content: The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) is a government-controlled organization in Pakistan tasked with combating the supply and distribution of narcotics, as well as organizing rehabilitation programs for drug users. The ANF is currently led by Director General Lieutenant General Shujaat Zamir Dar. Historical Background The Pakistan Narcotics Board (PNB) was established in 1957 under the Revenue Division to fulfill Pakistan's obligations under the International Opium Convention of 1925. The PNB included representatives from provincial governments and various federal ministries. Pakistan ratified the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs of 1961 on August 15, 1965. To meet its obligations under this convention, the government renamed the PNB as the Pakistan Narcotics Control Board (PNCB) on March 8, 1973. In December 1991, the Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) was created. Later, in February 1995, the PNCB and ANTF were merged to form the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF), which became the premier law enforcement agency for narcotics control in Pakistan. Responsibilities of the ANF The ANF is responsible for: 1. Coordinating efforts among law enforcement agencies to fulfill international obligations. 2. Striving to achieve a drug-free society. 3. Translating government objectives into actionable measures for narcotics control. Currently, the ANF operates with approximately 1,500 personnel, although its authorized strength is 2,552. Other organizations involved in narcotics control include the Airports Security Force, Pakistan Coast Guards, Customs, Provincial Excise and Taxation, Frontier Corps, Frontier Constabulary, Pakistan Rangers, Provincial Police, and Pakistan Railways Police. Narcotics Control Division In 1989, the Ministry of Interior established a separate Narcotics Control Division to exclusively handle drug-related matters. Policy Review Board In 1997, a Policy Review Board was established to monitor federal government policies on narcotics control. It is headed by the Minister for Narcotics Control and includes 14 members from relevant federal and provincial ministries. The composition of this board is under review due to the establishment of a separate ministry for narcotics control. Narcotics Interdiction Committee (NIC) The NIC was created to enhance the federal government's coordinating role and ensure synchronized efforts among various law enforcement agencies in narcotics interdiction. ANF's Charter of Duty The ANF's duties include: Supply Reduction: Limiting the smuggling, trafficking, and distribution of narcotics; eradicating opium poppy cultivation; preventing the operation of heroin labs; investigating the assets of drug barons; and pursuing legal cases relentlessly. Demand Reduction: Reducing the demand for illicit drugs through preventive education, treatment, rehabilitation, and harm reduction programs. Coordination: Enhancing international cooperation in the fight against drugs and liaising with organizations such as the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the International Narcotics Control Board, and other international agencies. National Drug Abuse Assessment Study (2000-2001) Over the past three decades, Pakistan has experienced a significant increase in the use of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. The government has implemented various measures to address this issue, but a comprehensive drug abuse control strategy required a realistic assessment of the problem's scope. The first National Survey on Drug Abuse (NSDA) was conducted in 1982, revealing a significant rise in heroin use and predicting a similar trend for the future. Subsequent surveys were conducted in 1984, 1986, 1988, and 1993. The most recent assessment, the National Drug Abuse Assessment Study (2000-2001), was conducted with the assistance of the United Nations Drug Control Programme (UNDCP). This study aimed to estimate the total population of hardcore heroin users, including intravenous drug users, and assess trends and patterns for other drug types. Key Findings of the Study 1. Prevalence: Among males aged 15-45, there are 500,000 regular heroin users and drug injectors, a rate alarmingly high by international standards. 2. Major Drugs of Abuse: Cannabis is the most commonly used drug in Pakistan, followed by heroin, alcohol, and psychotropic substances. 3. Urban vs. Rural Trends: Cannabis use is equally prevalent in urban and rural areas, while heroin abuse is more common in urban settings. 4. Education and Employment: On average, heroin users have six years of education. Among heroin users, 43% are unemployed, and 26% are engaged in full-time employment. 5. Age Group: Forty percent of heroin users fall within the 25-34 age bracket. 6. Occupational Grouping: Drug abuse is most prevalent among skilled and unskilled laborers (47%), followed by businesspersons (16%), agricultural workers (5%), and students (3%). 7. Financial Support: Among drug users, 22% sustain themselves through casual work, 18% rely on family support, 16% are beggars, 13% are drug peddlers, and 11% resort to petty thefts and pickpocketing. 8. Gender: Drug abuse is less common among women compared to men. Psychotropic substances are the most commonly abused drugs among women, who constitute only 3% of reported patients. 9. Problems Associated with Drug Abuse: Heroin is identified as the primary drug responsible for societal unrest, followed by alcohol. Cannabis, while widely used, is not perceived as a major cause of social upheaval, although cannabis-related issues have been reported in some areas. 10. Current Drug Use: Among heroin users, 77% use the drug daily. For hashish/charas, 41% use it daily, and 34% use it occasionally. Alcohol consumption is more varied, with 76% consuming it twice or thrice a week or less, and only 10% consuming it five or more days a week. 11. Methods of Administration: Seventy-three percent of heroin users smoke or inhale the drug, 11% sniff it, and 15% inject it. Injecting drug use is associated with a high risk of blood-borne infections. 12. Treatment and Rehabilitation: Sixty-four percent of respondents report difficulties in accessing treatment, with 80% citing affordability as a major barrier. A lack of in-patient facilities in government hospitals is a deterrent for 23% of respondents. Forty-four percent have received treatment for drug problems at some point, with 96% treated for heroin addiction. However, most addicts did not receive intensive or sustained therapy. 13. Prison Contact: Thirty-five percent of respondents have spent time in prison for drug-related offenses. International Obligations and Extradition Pakistan has ratified several United Nations conventions, including the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (1961), the Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971), and the Convention Against Illicit Trafficking in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (1988). Pakistan has also adopted extradition treaties concluded by the British government with 19 countries and has directly concluded extradition treaties with countries such as Australia, Iran, Maldives, Turkey, Egypt, Italy, Saudi Arabia, and Algeria. International Initiatives Pakistan has hosted several international meetings, including the Six Plus Two technical-level meeting in 2001, the Gulf Cooperation meeting in 2004, and the Paris Pact Expert Roundtable Conference in 2005. These efforts were co-sponsored by the ANF, Narcotics Affairs Section (NAS), and UNDCP. Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) To strengthen joint efforts against drug trafficking, Pakistan has signed MOUs with countries such as China, Iran, Russia, Egypt, Nigeria, UAE, Kyrgyzstan, Romania, and Uzbekistan. MOUs with Indonesia, Kuwait, Syria, Egypt, Morocco, and Thailand are in progress.
